issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
David, a 49-year-old city council member, presented as a man holding himself together with sheer force of will. He spoke in clipped, precise sentences about his life, his marriage, and his decorated military career, but when the conversation turned to why he was seeking help, his composure fractured. It had been over a decade since his last tour, but the event that brought him here felt as immediate as yesterday. During a house-clearing operation, his unit was ambushed in a narrow, dusty corridor. The chaos was absolute, a blur of motion and noise. What he remembers most clearly is the sudden, violent weight of an enemy combatant tackling him, and in the same instant, the feeling of his friend being pulled away from his side into the dark. He never saw his friend alive again.

The memory of that corridor does not exist as a coherent narrative for David. Instead, it erupts in sensory fragments: the rough texture of the wall scraping his cheek, the suffocating dust, the sudden, heavy impact on his back. When these images surface, they bring with them the same raw terror he felt at the time, a visceral certainty of imminent death. This bodily hijacking has convinced David that his own physical responses are an enemy, perpetually betraying him into a state of high alert even when he is sitting in his own quiet home. From this, he has concluded that the world is an irredeemably dangerous place and that he must remain on guard at all times, because an ambush could happen again, anywhere.

This pervasive sense of threat dictates the terms of his existence. He can go days on only a few hours of sleep, his body refusing to stand down. Lying in bed, his heart thuds against his ribs, and the slightest creak of the floorboards sends a jolt of adrenaline through him. In this state of heightened physical arousal, the fragmented images of the firefight return with startling clarity, feeling less like memories and more like active threats. This constant vigilance has cemented his fear that he is fundamentally broken, unable to trust his own senses or the reassurances of others. Even when his wife, Elena, tells him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe her; his body's alarm is too loud to ignore.

To manage the intrusions, David has developed a rigid set of strategies. The moment a fragment of memory surfaces at his desk at city hall, he immediately retreats to his office and turns on a television, blasting cable news at a volume that drowns out everything else. This sensory blitz shoves the memory back down, but the terror it produced lingers, unprocessed. The frantic effort to police his own mind-constantly monitoring his thoughts for any sign of "going crazy"-has only strengthened his conviction that he is losing control. By never allowing the memory to be fully examined, his avoidance ensures it retains its power, guaranteeing it will erupt again.

The consequences of this cycle have become untenable. As a public servant, his role requires him to be accessible, but the fear of being touched has made this nearly impossible. At a recent town hall, a constituent clapped him on the shoulder in gratitude, and David flinched so violently he knocked over a pitcher of water. He now avoids all physical contact, recoiling even from his wife's comforting hand on his arm. This has created a painful distance in his marriage and is beginning to damage his political career, as he increasingly sends aides to events he should be attending himself. The incomplete picture of the trauma haunts him; he feels that if he could just remember the whole sequence of events, he might be able to explain it clearly and rob it of its power, but every time he tries, he loses the thread, overwhelmed by sheer terror.

He came to therapy after Elena found him one morning at 3 a.m., standing in their living room, staring at the front door, convinced someone was trying to get in. She told him she couldn't watch him live in a war zone he'd long since left. David is terrified of losing her, but an even deeper fear is that his body is right-that the danger is real, and that letting his guard down for even a moment will be a fatal mistake.
